concept: Parallelization (concurrent LLM calls, DAG scheduling, speculative execution, map-reduce, ensembles)
summary:
Parallelization in LLM pipelines operates at three distinct levels, and the literature is clearest when they are kept separate. (1) Output-level and plan-level parallelism: a planner LLM emits a structure (a skeleton of answer points in Skeleton-of-Thought, a dependency DAG of tool calls in LLMCompiler, a set of sub-problems in Branch-Solve-Merge) and independent pieces are executed concurrently; verified gains are 2x-2.4x latency reduction for SoT across 12 models, up to 3.7x latency and 6.7x cost reduction over ReAct for LLMCompiler, and up to 26% higher human-LLM agreement for BSM. (2) Ensemble/sample-level parallelism: the same task is run N times (self-consistency, sampling-and-voting in "More Agents Is All You Need", repeated sampling in Large Language Monkeys) or across layered heterogeneous models (Mixture-of-Agents, Archon) and results are aggregated by vote, LLM-judged consistency (Universal Self-Consistency), verifiers, or a final aggregator; gains are large and roughly log-linear in sample count for verifiable domains (SWE-bench Lite 15.9% -> 56% with 250 samples) but saturate at several hundred samples for unverifiable ones, and mixing weaker models can hurt (Self-MoA beats MoA by 6.6% on AlpacaEval 2.0). (3) Inference-level parallelism inside the serving engine: speculative decoding (2-3x), Medusa heads (2.2-3.6x), continuous/iteration-level batching (Orca, 36.9x throughput vs FasterTransformer), PagedAttention (vLLM, 2-4x throughput over Orca), RadixAttention prefix sharing (SGLang, up to 6.4x), and application-level dataflow scheduling (Parrot semantic variables, up to an order of magnitude end-to-end). Clients cannot control level 3 directly, but its existence dictates client design: shared-prefix requests, warm-then-burst fan-out, structured programs rather than isolated calls, and batching of latency-tolerant work.

The engineering half of the state of the art is older and comes from distributed systems: Amdahl's law bounds the speedup at 1/(1-p) where p is the parallelizable fraction, so the serial planner-plus-aggregator path, not the fan-out, determines wall-clock; MapReduce (Dean & Ghemawat 2004) established fault tolerance via deterministic, re-executable tasks; The Tail at Scale (Dean & Barroso 2013) established hedged and tied requests for tail latency; Brooker's AWS analysis established full-jitter exponential backoff; the Google SRE book established retry budgets (3 attempts per request, retries under 10% of traffic), client-side adaptive throttling (K=2), criticality-based load shedding and deadline propagation; and Nygard's Release It! codified circuit breakers, bulkheads, timeouts and backpressure. Provider documentation adds the LLM-specific constraints: token-bucket rate limiting with 429/retry-after, cache-aware input-token limits, prompt caches that become available only after the first response begins (so a naive parallel burst misses the cache), a tools -> system -> messages cache hierarchy, and a 50%-discounted asynchronous Batch API for latency-tolerant fan-out. Anthropic's own multi-agent research system shows the economics: parallel orchestrator-worker systems improved an internal research eval by 90.2% and cut research time by up to 90%, but used roughly 15x the tokens of a chat interaction, so parallelism must be gated by task value and by Amdahl-style critical-path analysis.

papers.title: Skeleton-of-Thought: Prompting LLMs for Efficient Parallel Generation
papers.authors: Xuefei Ning, Zinan Lin, Zixuan Zhou, Zifu Wang, Huazhong Yang, Yu Wang
papers.citation_signal: ICLR 2024 acceptance; widely cited as the canonical output-level parallel generation method; reproduced in many agent frameworks
papers.key_contribution: Two-stage prompting: the LLM first emits a short skeleton (list of answer points), then each point is expanded in parallel via concurrent API calls or batched decoding. Speed-ups of up to 2.39x across 12 LLMs (over 2x on 8 of 12), e.g. Claude 22s -> 12s (1.83x), Vicuna-33B 43s -> 16s (2.69x) on an A100, evaluated on Vicuna-80 (80 questions, 9 categories) and WizardLM. Quality is at least as good as normal decoding in roughly 60% of cases, helping diversity/relevance but hurting coherence; it performs poorly on writing, Fermi, math and coding where later steps depend on earlier ones. SoT-R adds a router (GPT-4 prompt or a ~120M RoBERTa classifier) that triggers SoT only on suitable questions and otherwise falls back to sequential decoding.
papers.design_implication: Implement skeleton-then-expand as a first-class execution strategy, but gate it with a router that predicts whether answer points are independent; route math, code, step-by-step derivations and narrative writing to sequential generation. Expansions should run as a concurrent fan-out sharing an identical cached prefix (question + skeleton), and the merge step should be a deterministic concatenation with an optional light coherence pass.

papers.title: An LLM Compiler for Parallel Function Calling
papers.authors: Sehoon Kim, Suhong Moon, Ryan Tabrizi, Nicholas Lee, Michael W. Mahoney, Kurt Keutzer, Amir Gholami
papers.citation_signal: ICML 2024; several hundred citations; integrated into LangGraph/LlamaIndex examples; the reference design for DAG-based parallel tool use
papers.key_contribution: Three components: a Function Calling Planner that emits a DAG of tasks with placeholder variables for dependencies, a Task Fetching Unit that dispatches tasks as soon as their inputs resolve, and an Executor that runs independent tasks concurrently, plus dynamic replanning when intermediate results require new tasks. Versus ReAct: HotpotQA 1.80x latency / 3.37x cost (GPT-3.5); Movie Recommendation 3.74x latency / 6.73x cost with accuracy 68.6 -> 77.1; ParallelQA 2.15x / 4.65x (GPT-4-turbo); Game of 24 2.89x vs Tree-of-Thoughts at 75.3% accuracy; WebShop success 35.2 -> 55.6 (GPT-4). Documents ReAct failure modes: early stopping on incomplete information (~85% of Movie Recommendation examples) and repetitive function calls (~10% of HotpotQA needing >4 calls, often looping).
papers.design_implication: The core of a production parallelization component should be a planner -> DAG -> dependency-aware scheduler -> concurrent executor loop, with explicit variable binding (e.g. $1, $2 placeholders) resolved at dispatch time, and a bounded replanning loop. Plan once and execute many rather than interleaving reason/act per call; this is where most latency and cost reduction comes from.

papers.title: Branch-Solve-Merge Improves Large Language Model Evaluation and Generation
papers.authors: Swarnadeep Saha, Omer Levy, Asli Celikyilmaz, Mohit Bansal, Jason Weston, Xian Li
papers.citation_signal: NAACL 2024 main conference; Meta FAIR authorship; widely cited for parallel decomposition in LLM-as-judge
papers.key_contribution: A branch module prompts the LLM to decompose a task into parallel, independent sub-tasks (e.g. evaluation criteria or story constraints), a solve module answers each branch independently, and a merge module combines them. On LLM response evaluation with Vicuna, LLaMA-2-chat and GPT-4, BSM raises human-LLM agreement by up to 26% and reduces length and pairwise position bias by up to 50%; LLaMA-2-chat with BSM matches or beats GPT-4 on most domains. On constrained story generation, constraint satisfaction improves by 12%.
papers.design_implication: Branch-solve-merge is the general-purpose map-reduce for judgement and multi-constraint generation: let the model propose the branches (criteria, sections, constraints), run solves concurrently, and merge with a dedicated prompt. Use it for verification/evaluation fan-out and for multi-section documents such as specs and reports; it also mitigates evaluator biases that single-call judges exhibit.

papers.title: Mixture-of-Agents Enhances Large Language Model Capabilities
papers.authors: Junlin Wang, Jue Wang, Ben Athiwaratkun, Ce Zhang, James Zou
papers.citation_signal: ICLR 2025 main conference; Together AI production deployment; hundreds of citations
papers.key_contribution: Layered ensemble: each layer runs several proposer LLMs in parallel, each conditioned on all outputs of the previous layer, and a final aggregator synthesizes. Default configuration is 3 layers x 6 open-source proposers (Qwen1.5-110B/72B-Chat, WizardLM-8x22B, LLaMA-3-70B-Instruct, Mixtral-8x22B, dbrx-instruct) with Qwen1.5-110B as aggregator, reaching 65.1% on AlpacaEval 2.0 vs 57.5% for GPT-4o; also SOTA on MT-Bench and FLASK. Documents 'collaborativeness': models improve when shown other models' outputs even when those are weaker. MoA-Lite (2 layers, Qwen1.5-72B aggregator) beats GPT-4o by ~1.8% at similar cost. Limitation: sequential layers give a high time-to-first-token.
papers.design_implication: Implement a layered proposer/aggregator ensemble as an optional 'quality mode' for high-value, latency-tolerant tasks; proposers within a layer run concurrently and the aggregator prompt must instruct critical synthesis rather than averaging. Expose layer count and proposer set as configuration, defaulting to the cheaper 2-layer variant, and measure TTFT because layers are serial.

papers.title: More Agents Is All You Need
papers.authors: Junyou Li, Qin Zhang, Yangbin Yu, Qiang Fu, Deheng Ye
papers.venue: Transactions on Machine Learning Research (TMLR) 2024 (arXiv Feb 2024)
papers.citation_signal: TMLR publication; Tencent authorship; hundreds of citations; frequently cited as the scaling-law reference for sampling-and-voting
papers.key_contribution: A simple sampling-and-voting method ('Agent Forest'): sample N answers in parallel, majority-vote. Ensembles up to 40 agents, averaged over 10 runs. Gains from 1 -> 40 agents: GSM8K +12% to +24% (Llama2-13B 0.35 -> 0.59, Llama2-70B 0.54 -> 0.74), MATH +6% to +10%, MMLU +5% to +11%, HumanEval +4% to +9%, Chess +1% to +4%. Llama2-13B with ~15 agents matches single-query Llama2-70B; GPT-3.5 matches its stronger counterpart at ~20 agents. Gains rise then fall with task difficulty, tapering where the task exceeds the model's capacity. Debate baselines were capped at 10 agents because of communication overhead.
papers.design_implication: Parallel sampling with majority vote is the cheapest reliable quality lever and should be the default ensemble mode; set N adaptively (5-10 for most tasks, 15-40 only for hard, well-verifiable tasks) and stop early when a vote is decisive. Prefer independent samples over debate for throughput; debate's cross-agent communication is serial and expensive.

papers.title: Self-Consistency Improves Chain of Thought Reasoning in Language Models
papers.authors: Xuezhi Wang, Jason Wei, Dale Schuurmans, Quoc Le, Ed Chi, Sharan Narang, Aakanksha Chowdhery, Denny Zhou
papers.citation_signal: ICLR 2023; thousands of citations; foundational for all vote-based ensembles
papers.key_contribution: Replaces greedy decoding with sampling multiple diverse reasoning paths in parallel and selecting the most consistent final answer by marginalizing over paths (majority vote on extracted answers). Gains over CoT: GSM8K +17.9%, SVAMP +11.0%, AQuA +12.2%, StrategyQA +6.4%, ARC-challenge +3.9%.
papers.design_implication: Any parallel sampling path needs a deterministic answer extractor and a vote; the component should carry a pluggable 'canonicalize answer' function per domain (numeric normalization, code AST normalization, JSON key ordering) so votes compare equal answers. Temperature must be > 0 for diversity; run samples as a concurrent batch sharing the cached prompt prefix.

papers.title: Universal Self-Consistency for Large Language Model Generation
papers.authors: Xinyun Chen, Renat Aksitov, Uri Alon, Jie Ren, Kefan Xiao, Pengcheng Yin, Sushant Prakash, Charles Sutton, Xuezhi Wang, Denny Zhou
papers.citation_signal: Google DeepMind; several hundred citations; standard method for aggregating free-form parallel samples
papers.key_contribution: Universal Self-Consistency (USC) feeds all sampled candidates back to the LLM and asks it to select the most consistent one, removing the need for a shared answer format. Matches standard self-consistency on math, matches execution-based voting on code without executing, and extends consistency-based aggregation to long-context summarization and open-ended QA where answer extraction is impossible.
papers.design_implication: Use USC as the aggregator when outputs are free-form (summaries, specs, incident write-ups, design rationales) and exact-match voting is undefined. It costs one extra call whose input scales with N x answer length, so cap N (typically 5-8) and truncate candidates consistently.

papers.title: Tree of Thoughts: Deliberate Problem Solving with Large Language Models
papers.authors: Shunyu Yao, Dian Yu, Jeffrey Zhao, Izhak Shafran, Thomas L. Griffiths, Yuan Cao, Karthik Narasimhan
papers.citation_signal: NeurIPS 2023; thousands of citations; canonical search-over-thoughts framework
papers.key_contribution: Generalizes CoT to a tree: at each step the model proposes several candidate 'thoughts', self-evaluates them, and a search algorithm (BFS keeping the best b states, or DFS with backtracking) chooses which to expand. Game of 24 success rises from 4% (GPT-4 CoT) to 74%; also evaluated on Creative Writing and Mini Crosswords.
papers.design_implication: BFS over thoughts is an embarrassingly parallel frontier expansion: all proposals and all evaluations at a depth can be issued concurrently, then pruned. Implement ToT as a DAG-per-depth with configurable breadth, depth and an evaluator; LLMCompiler shows the same search runs ~2-2.9x faster when proposer/evaluator calls are scheduled in parallel.

papers.title: Large Language Monkeys: Scaling Inference Compute with Repeated Sampling
papers.authors: Bradley Brown, Jordan Juravsky, Ryan Ehrlich, Ronald Clark, Quoc V. Le, Christopher Re, Azalia Mirhoseini
papers.citation_signal: Several hundred citations; the standard reference for coverage scaling with repeated sampling
papers.key_contribution: Coverage (fraction of problems solved by at least one of N samples) scales log-linearly with N over four orders of magnitude, modeled by an exponentiated power law. SWE-bench Lite with DeepSeek-Coder-V2-Instruct: 15.9% with 1 sample -> 56% with 250 samples, beating the 43% single-sample SOTA. In verifiable domains (code with tests, formal proofs) coverage converts directly to accuracy; in unverifiable domains, majority voting and reward models plateau beyond several hundred samples.
papers.design_implication: The value of parallel sampling depends on whether a verifier exists. For code, calculations and anything with executable checks, scale N aggressively and select by verifier; for free-form outputs cap N low because voting saturates. The component should therefore expose a 'verifiability' flag per task that controls the sample budget.

papers.title: Scaling LLM Test-Time Compute Optimally can be More Effective than Scaling Model Parameters
papers.authors: Charlie Snell, Jaehoon Lee, Kelvin Xu, Aviral Kumar
papers.venue: arXiv preprint (UC Berkeley / Google DeepMind), Aug 2024
papers.citation_signal: Hundreds of citations; the reference for compute-optimal allocation of parallel vs sequential inference compute
papers.key_contribution: Compares parallel search against process reward models with sequential revision under a fixed compute budget. The best strategy depends on prompt difficulty; a 'compute-optimal' per-prompt allocation improves efficiency by more than 4x over best-of-N, and in FLOPs-matched comparisons lets a smaller model beat one 14x larger on problems where the small model has non-trivial success rates.
papers.design_implication: Do not use a fixed fan-out: estimate difficulty (cheap classifier or first-sample disagreement) and allocate parallel samples adaptively, spending more on medium-difficulty tasks and falling back to sequential revision or a larger model when parallel sampling cannot help.

papers.title: Rethinking Mixture-of-Agents: Is Mixing Different Large Language Models Beneficial?
papers.authors: Wenzhe Li, Yong Lin, Mengzhou Xia, Chi Jin
papers.citation_signal: Princeton authorship; directly challenges the ICLR 2025 MoA result and sets a new AlpacaEval 2.0 SOTA; the documented pitfall paper for heterogeneous ensembles
papers.key_contribution: Self-MoA aggregates N samples from the single best model instead of mixing models. It beats MoA by 6.6% on AlpacaEval 2.0 and by 3.8% on average across MMLU, CRUX and MATH. MoA performance is highly sensitive to proposer quality and mixing 'often lowers the average quality'; a quality-diversity tradeoff exists with limited scenarios where mixing helps. A sequential Self-MoA that aggregates in rounds matches aggregating all outputs at once.
papers.design_implication: Default the ensemble to homogeneous sampling from the strongest available model and only enable heterogeneous proposers when evaluation data shows the mixed set's average quality is close to the best model. Treat 'diversity' as a hypothesis to test, not a free win.

papers.title: Archon: An Architecture Search Framework for Inference-Time Techniques
papers.authors: Jon Saad-Falcon, Adrian Gamarra Lafuente, Shlok Natarajan, Nahum Maru, Hristo Todorov, Etash Guha, E. Kelly Buchanan, Mayee Chen, Neel Guha, Christopher Re, Azalia Mirhoseini
papers.citation_signal: ICML 2025; Stanford Hazy Research; the reference for automated composition of parallel inference-time techniques
papers.key_contribution: Models inference-time techniques (generation ensembles, repeated sampling, ranking, fusion, critique, verification, unit-test generation) as composable layers and searches the configuration space under a compute budget. Archon-designed systems outperform o1, GPT-4o and Claude 3.5 Sonnet by an average of 15.1% across instruction-following, reasoning and coding benchmarks.
papers.design_implication: Make the parallel topology (fan-out width, number of layers, aggregator type, verifier presence) a declarative configuration that can be searched offline against a task-specific eval set, rather than hand-tuned once. This is how a task-agnostic component becomes task-optimal per domain.

papers.title: Fast Inference from Transformers via Speculative Decoding
papers.authors: Yaniv Leviathan, Matan Kalman, Yossi Matias
papers.citation_signal: ICML 2023 oral; over a thousand citations; the foundational speculative decoding paper, implemented in vLLM, TGI, TensorRT-LLM
papers.key_contribution: A small draft model proposes K tokens; the large model verifies them in one parallel forward pass and accepts via a rejection-sampling rule that provably preserves the target distribution, with no retraining or architecture change. 2x-3x acceleration on T5-XXL with identical outputs.
papers.design_implication: Speculative execution at the token level is a server-side optimization; the client implication is that per-token latency varies with draft acceptance rate, which depends on how predictable the output is. Structured, templated outputs (JSON, code boilerplate) accelerate more; clients should not assume constant tokens/sec when sizing timeouts.

papers.title: Accelerating Large Language Model Decoding with Speculative Sampling
papers.authors: Charlie Chen, Sebastian Borgeaud, Geoffrey Irving, Jean-Baptiste Lespiau, Laurent Sifre, John Jumper
papers.citation_signal: DeepMind; hundreds of citations; independently derived the same speculative sampling result as Leviathan et al. and validated it at 70B scale
papers.key_contribution: Draft model proposes a short continuation; the 70B Chinchilla target scores all draft tokens in parallel in about the time of one token; a modified rejection sampling scheme preserves the target distribution within numerical precision. 2-2.5x decoding speedup in a distributed setup with no quality loss.
papers.design_implication: Confirms speculative decoding works at production scale on distributed serving; when self-hosting, enable it in the engine (vLLM supports n-gram, EAGLE and other drafters). Clients benefit most when they stream and consume tokens incrementally rather than waiting for complete responses.

papers.title: Medusa: Simple LLM Inference Acceleration Framework with Multiple Decoding Heads
papers.authors: Tianle Cai, Yuhong Li, Zhengyang Geng, Hongwu Peng, Jason D. Lee, Deming Chen, Tri Dao
papers.citation_signal: Several hundred citations; implemented in TensorRT-LLM, vLLM and TGI; the main draft-model-free speculative method
papers.key_contribution: Adds extra decoding heads to the base model to predict several future tokens at once and verifies candidate continuations with tree attention in a single step, removing the need for a separate draft model. Medusa-1 (frozen backbone) gives over 2.2x lossless speedup; Medusa-2 (joint fine-tuning) gives 2.3-3.6x; includes self-distillation when no training data exists and a 'typical acceptance' scheme.
papers.design_implication: For self-hosted engineering assistants where a draft model is operationally burdensome, Medusa-style heads are the practical route to 2-3x decode speedup. Tree-based verification is the same idea as tree-of-thoughts at token granularity: propose many, verify in parallel, keep the best path.

papers.title: SpecInfer: Accelerating Generative Large Language Model Serving with Tree-based Speculative Inference and Verification
papers.authors: Xupeng Miao, Gabriele Oliaro, Zhihao Zhang, Xinhao Cheng, Zeyu Wang, et al. (Zhihao Jia)
papers.citation_signal: ASPLOS 2024; several hundred citations; introduced token-tree verification adopted by Medusa, EAGLE and others
papers.key_contribution: Multiple small speculative models produce a token tree; the LLM verifies all candidate sequences in parallel with tree-based parallel decoding, acting as a verifier rather than an incremental decoder. 1.5-2.8x speedup for distributed inference and 2.6-3.5x for offloading-based inference with unchanged outputs.
papers.design_implication: Reinforces the general pattern for the component: cheap proposers fan out, an expensive verifier checks all proposals in one batched step. The same propose-many/verify-once structure should be used at the task level (cheap model drafts, strong model verifies in parallel).

papers.title: Orca: A Distributed Serving System for Transformer-Based Generative Models
papers.authors: Gyeong-In Yu, Joo Seong Jeong, Geon-Woo Kim, Soojeong Kim, Byung-Gon Chun
papers.citation_signal: OSDI 2022; the paper that introduced continuous (iteration-level) batching, now standard in vLLM, TGI, TensorRT-LLM and all major providers
papers.key_contribution: Iteration-level scheduling runs one model iteration at a time so finished requests leave the batch and new arrivals join immediately, instead of waiting for whole-batch completion; selective batching applies batching only to operators where it is valid. 36.9x throughput improvement over NVIDIA FasterTransformer at the same latency on GPT-3 175B.
papers.design_implication: Because servers batch at the iteration level, many concurrent client requests are nearly free in throughput terms relative to sequential calls; the cost of fan-out is dominated by tokens, rate limits and tail latency, not by server inefficiency. Clients should issue independent requests concurrently and let the server batch them.

papers.title: Efficient Memory Management for Large Language Model Serving with PagedAttention
papers.authors: Woosuk Kwon, Zhuohan Li, Siyuan Zhuang, Ying Sheng, Lianmin Zheng, Cody Hao Yu, Joseph E. Gonzalez, Hao Zhang, Ion Stoica
papers.citation_signal: SOSP 2023; thousands of citations; vLLM is the dominant open-source serving engine
papers.key_contribution: PagedAttention manages the KV cache in non-contiguous blocks like OS virtual memory pages, eliminating fragmentation and enabling KV sharing across requests (e.g. parallel sampling from one prompt). vLLM achieves 2-4x throughput over FasterTransformer and Orca at the same latency, with larger gains for longer sequences, larger models and complex decoding such as parallel sampling and beam search.
papers.design_implication: Parallel sampling (n candidates from one prompt) is specifically cheap on PagedAttention engines because the prompt KV is shared; when self-hosting, request n samples in a single call rather than n separate calls. Prefix caching in vLLM extends this across requests that share a prefix.

papers.title: Parrot: Efficient Serving of LLM-based Applications with Semantic Variable
papers.authors: Chaofan Lin, Zhenhua Han, Chengruidong Zhang, Yuqing Yang, Fan Yang, Chen Chen, Lili Qiu
papers.citation_signal: OSDI 2024 (Microsoft Research); the systems-venue argument for exposing application dataflow to the serving layer
papers.key_contribution: Introduces the Semantic Variable: annotated input/output placeholders in prompts that connect multiple LLM requests into a dataflow pipeline, letting the service perform data-flow analysis across requests (dependency discovery, shared-prefix detection, scheduling of independent requests together). Reports up to an order-of-magnitude end-to-end improvement on popular LLM application patterns versus request-at-a-time serving.
papers.design_implication: Represent pipeline steps as a typed dataflow graph with named variables (not opaque strings) so the executor can detect independence, co-schedule shared-prefix requests, and pipe outputs to inputs without round-tripping through the orchestrator. This also makes the DAG inspectable and testable.

papers.title: SGLang: Efficient Execution of Structured Language Model Programs
papers.authors: Lianmin Zheng, Liangsheng Yin, Zhiqiang Xie, Chuyue Sun, Jeff Huang, Cody Hao Yu, Shiyi Cao, Christos Kozyrakis, Ion Stoica, Joseph E. Gonzalez, Clark Barrett, Ying Sheng
papers.citation_signal: NeurIPS 2024 main track (proceedings.neurips.cc); SGLang is a widely deployed serving engine (xAI, LMSYS); ranked among most influential NeurIPS 2024 papers by Paper Digest
papers.key_contribution: A frontend DSL with primitives for generation and parallelism control (fork/join of program branches) and a runtime with RadixAttention (radix-tree KV cache reuse across requests sharing prefixes) and compressed finite-state machines for fast constrained decoding. Up to 6.4x higher throughput than state-of-the-art systems on agent control, logical reasoning, few-shot learning, JSON decoding, RAG and multi-turn chat.
papers.design_implication: Fan-outs that share a long prefix (same system prompt, same document, different sub-questions) should be structured so the shared part is a true byte-identical prefix; on SGLang/vLLM this gives automatic KV reuse and on hosted APIs it maps to prompt caching. Use constrained/structured decoding for branch outputs so the merge step can parse them deterministically.

papers.title: Asynchronous LLM Function Calling
papers.authors: In Gim, Seung-seob Lee, Lin Zhong
papers.citation_signal: Recent; evaluated on the Berkeley Function Calling Leaderboard; the clearest treatment of non-blocking tool calls with interrupts
papers.key_contribution: AsyncLM lets the model continue generating while function calls execute, using an in-context protocol for issuing calls and receiving interrupt notifications when results return, plus a fine-tuning recipe. Reduces end-to-end task latency by 1.6x-5.4x versus synchronous function calling on BFCL tasks.
papers.design_implication: Even without model fine-tuning, the executor should be fully asynchronous: dispatch tool calls as soon as the model emits them (streaming), continue parsing further calls, and feed results back as they arrive. Design the tool-result protocol around call_ids so out-of-order completion is safe.

papers.title: ReWOO: Decoupling Reasoning from Observations for Efficient Augmented Language Models
papers.authors: Binfeng Xu, Zhiyuan Peng, Bowen Lei, Subhabrata Mukherjee, Yuchen Liu, Dongkuan Xu
papers.citation_signal: Several hundred citations; implemented in LangChain/LangGraph as the plan-and-execute agent
papers.key_contribution: Plans all tool calls up front (Planner), executes them without re-invoking the LLM per observation (Worker), then synthesizes (Solver). 5x token efficiency and +4% accuracy on HotpotQA versus interleaved ReAct, consistent gains on six benchmarks, robustness to tool failure, and distillation of planning from GPT-3.5 into a 7B LLaMA.
papers.design_implication: Plan-then-execute is the precondition for parallel tool execution: once the plan is explicit, independent steps can be dispatched concurrently and the model is not in the critical path per step. Include tool-failure handling in the solver prompt so partial results still yield an answer.

papers.title: Learning Adaptive Parallel Reasoning with Language Models
papers.authors: Jiayi Pan, Xiuyu Li, Long Lian, Charlie Snell, Yifei Zhou, Adam Yala, Trevor Darrell, Kurt Keutzer, Alane Suhr
papers.citation_signal: COLM 2025 acceptance; UC Berkeley; represents the newest direction of model-controlled spawn/join parallelism
papers.key_contribution: Adaptive Parallel Reasoning trains a model to orchestrate its own serial and parallel computation via spawn() and join() operations, with parent and child threads trained jointly by end-to-end RL. On Countdown: 83.4% vs 60.0% at a 4k context window, 80.1% vs 66.6% at 20k total tokens, and 75.2% vs 57.3% at matched ~5s latency.
papers.design_implication: Expose spawn/join as primitives in the component's execution API so that either the orchestrator code or the model itself can request child tasks; this keeps the architecture compatible with models trained to parallelize their own reasoning.

papers.title: LLM x MapReduce: Simplified Long-Sequence Processing using Large Language Models
papers.authors: Zihan Zhou, Chong Li, Xinyi Chen, Shuo Wang, Yu Chao, et al. (Zhiyuan Liu, Maosong Sun)
papers.citation_signal: Tsinghua NLP (OpenBMB); the most explicit treatment of failure modes in LLM map-reduce over long documents
papers.key_contribution: Training-free divide-and-conquer: split a long document into chunks processed in parallel (map), then aggregate (reduce). Identifies two failure modes of naive chunking, inter-chunk dependencies and inter-chunk conflicts, and addresses them with a structured information protocol (each map emits extracted info, rationale, answer and confidence) and in-context confidence calibration for the reduce step. Outperforms representative open-source and commercial long-context LLMs.
papers.design_implication: When map-reducing over specs, standards, logs or incident timelines, require each mapper to emit a structured record (evidence, rationale, answer, calibrated confidence) rather than free text, and have the reducer resolve conflicts using those confidences. Add overlap or a shared global summary to mitigate cross-chunk dependencies.

papers.title: Improving Factuality and Reasoning in Language Models through Multiagent Debate
papers.authors: Yilun Du, Shuang Li, Antonio Torralba, Joshua B. Tenenbaum, Igor Mordatch
papers.citation_signal: Over a thousand citations; the canonical multi-agent debate paper
papers.key_contribution: Multiple LLM instances answer independently, then read each other's answers and revise over several rounds, converging on a final answer. Improves mathematical and strategic reasoning and reduces factual errors and hallucinations with the same prompts across tasks and black-box models.
papers.design_implication: Debate is a parallel-then-sequential pattern: round 1 is embarrassingly parallel, later rounds are serial and each round's input grows with the number of agents. Use it sparingly (2-3 agents, 2 rounds) for factuality-critical outputs; More Agents Is All You Need found simple voting scales more cheaply.

papers.title: DSPy: Compiling Declarative Language Model Calls into Self-Improving Pipelines
papers.authors: Omar Khattab, Arnav Singhvi, Paridhi Maheshwari, Zhiyuan Zhang, Keshav Santhanam, et al. (Matei Zaharia, Christopher Potts)
papers.venue: arXiv preprint (Stanford), Oct 2023; open-source library stanfordnlp/dspy
papers.citation_signal: Over a thousand citations; dspy library with wide industry adoption
papers.key_contribution: Represents LM pipelines as graphs of declarative modules with signatures; a compiler optimizes prompts/demonstrations against a metric. GPT-3.5 and llama2-13b-chat pipelines bootstrapped by DSPy beat few-shot prompting by over 25% and 65% respectively, and expert-written demonstrations by 5-46% and 16-40%; small models (770M T5, llama2-13b) become competitive with expert prompt chains on GPT-3.5.
papers.design_implication: Define each parallel branch (planner, mapper, verifier, aggregator) as a module with a typed signature so prompts can be optimized per domain without changing the DAG, and so the scheduler can treat modules as pure functions that are safe to run concurrently and to re-execute on failure.

papers.title: Validity of the single processor approach to achieving large scale computing capabilities
papers.authors: Gene M. Amdahl
papers.venue: AFIPS Spring Joint Computer Conference 1967, pp. 483-485 (DOI 10.1145/1465482.1465560)
papers.citation_signal: Foundational classic of parallel computing; tens of thousands of citations; taught in every parallel systems course
papers.key_contribution: Speedup S = 1 / ((1 - p) + p/s), where p is the fraction of work that can be sped up and s the speedup of that fraction. As s -> infinity, S -> 1/(1 - p): with 50% parallelizable work the ceiling is 2x, with 95% it is 20x. The serial fraction bounds total speedup regardless of parallel resources.
papers.design_implication: In an LLM pipeline the serial fraction is the planner call, the aggregator/merge call and any sequential tool chain; these dominate wall-clock once fan-out exceeds a few branches. Measure the critical path, minimize planner and aggregator latency (small/fast models, cached prefixes, streaming), and stop adding parallel branches when the critical path is already serial-bound.

papers.title: MapReduce: Simplified Data Processing on Large Clusters
papers.authors: Jeffrey Dean, Sanjay Ghemawat
papers.citation_signal: Foundational classic; tens of thousands of citations; basis of Hadoop and the map-reduce prompting pattern
papers.key_contribution: User-defined map (input pair -> intermediate pairs) and reduce (merge values per key) functions are automatically parallelized across commodity clusters; the runtime handles partitioning, scheduling, machine failures and communication, with thousands of jobs per day at Google. Failed workers' tasks are re-executed; because tasks are deterministic functions of their inputs, re-execution is correct and idempotent.
papers.design_implication: Model LLM fan-out tasks as pure, deterministic-as-possible functions of their inputs (fixed prompt, seed where available, no hidden state), persist intermediate outputs, and recover from partial failure by re-executing only failed branches. The merge step should be associative where possible so hierarchical (tree) reduction can be used for large fan-outs.

papers.title: The Tail at Scale
papers.authors: Jeffrey Dean, Luiz Andre Barroso
papers.venue: Communications of the ACM, vol. 56, no. 2, pp. 74-80
papers.citation_signal: Thousands of citations; standard reference for tail-latency engineering in fan-out systems
papers.key_contribution: Latency variability is amplified by fan-out: when a request depends on many parallel sub-requests, the slowest one determines completion, so rare slow responses become common at the request level. Proposes tail-tolerant techniques, notably hedged requests (issue a duplicate to another replica after the first has exceeded a delay such as the 95th-percentile expected latency, and cancel the loser) and tied requests (duplicates that cancel each other on start), which reuse resources already deployed for fault tolerance. (Hedging-at-p95 detail confirmed via secondary summaries of the paper.)
papers.design_implication: A fan-out of N LLM calls has completion time equal to the max of N latencies, so p99 of a 10-way fan-out is driven by the per-call p99.9. Implement hedged requests for idempotent calls (re-issue after the observed p95, cancel the loser), cap hedging to a small fraction of traffic, and use per-branch timeouts with deadline propagation.

papers.title: Exponential Backoff And Jitter
papers.authors: Marc Brooker (AWS)
papers.venue: AWS Architecture Blog (updated 2023 noting AWS SDK adoption)
papers.citation_signal: The de facto industry reference for retry timing; adopted in AWS SDKs and most HTTP client libraries
papers.key_contribution: Simulates contention under retries. Capped exponential backoff without jitter leaves clusters of synchronized retries; full jitter (sleep = random(0, min(cap, base*2^attempt))) does the least total work; decorrelated jitter finishes slightly sooner but makes more calls; equal jitter is slower. Un-jittered backoff is worst on both calls and completion time; jittered backoff should be standard for remote clients.
papers.design_implication: Use full-jitter exponential backoff for 429/529/5xx and connection errors on every LLM and tool call, honoring the provider's retry-after header when present as the floor. Never use fixed or un-jittered delays in a fan-out, because N branches failing together will retry together.

papers.title: Site Reliability Engineering: Handling Overload; Addressing Cascading Failures
papers.authors: Alejandro Forero Cuervo; Mike Ulrich (eds. Beyer, Jones, Petoff, Murphy)
papers.citation_signal: Industry-standard operations text from Google; the reference for retry budgets, criticality and load shedding
papers.key_contribution: Client-side adaptive throttling: track requests and accepts over 2 minutes and locally reject with increasing probability once requests exceed K x accepts (K=2 recommended). Retries: at most 3 attempts per request, a per-client retry budget of 10% of requests (bounding worst-case amplification to ~1.1x instead of 3x), an explicit 'overloaded; don't retry' signal, and retrying only at the layer directly above the failure to avoid combinatorial amplification (4 attempts at each of 3 layers = 64 database attempts). Four criticality levels (CRITICAL_PLUS, CRITICAL, SHEDDABLE_PLUS, SHEDDABLE) with lower levels shed first. Deadlines on every RPC, propagated down the call tree with cancellation; queues kept small (about 50% of thread pool or less) for steady traffic.
papers.design_implication: The parallel executor needs a global retry budget, per-request attempt cap, deadline propagation into every branch and tool, cancellation of in-flight siblings when a deadline or the parent is abandoned, and a criticality tag so speculative/hedged/ensemble work is shed before primary work under rate-limit pressure.

papers.title: Release It! Second Edition: Design and Deploy Production-Ready Software
papers.authors: Michael T. Nygard
papers.citation_signal: Industry classic that named the Circuit Breaker and Bulkhead patterns; implemented in Hystrix, Resilience4j, Polly, Envoy
papers.key_contribution: Catalogs stability patterns: Timeouts, Circuit Breaker (trip after repeated failures, fail fast while open, probe in half-open), Bulkheads (partition resources so one failing dependency cannot exhaust the pool), Steady State, Fail Fast, Handshaking, Let It Crash, Decoupling Middleware, Shed Load, Create Back Pressure and Governor.
papers.design_implication: Wrap each model endpoint and each tool in its own circuit breaker and bulkhead (separate concurrency pools) so a degraded provider or slow tool cannot stall the whole DAG; apply backpressure from the rate limiter to the planner so it does not emit more branches than can be executed within the deadline.

papers.title: Building effective agents
papers.authors: Erik Schluntz, Barry Zhang (Anthropic)
papers.citation_signal: Widely referenced industry taxonomy of agentic workflow patterns; basis for many framework designs
papers.key_contribution: Defines composable workflow patterns: prompt chaining with gates, routing, parallelization in two forms (sectioning: independent subtasks run concurrently, e.g. guardrail model alongside the answering model, or multi-aspect evals; voting: same task run several times with a vote threshold, e.g. multi-prompt vulnerability review), orchestrator-workers (dynamic subtask generation and synthesis, for multi-file code changes and multi-source search), and evaluator-optimizer loops. Advises the simplest approach that works and adding complexity only when it measurably helps.
papers.design_implication: Expose exactly these modes in the component's API (sectioning, voting, orchestrator-workers) with a router that picks the mode from the task prompt, and keep aggregation in code where possible (threshold votes, deterministic merges) rather than always in another LLM call.

papers.title: How we built our multi-agent research system
papers.authors: Anthropic engineering team
papers.citation_signal: Production postmortem-style report from a shipped system; frequently cited for multi-agent cost/benefit numbers
papers.key_contribution: Orchestrator-worker architecture with a lead agent spawning parallel search subagents and a separate citation agent. Opus 4 lead + Sonnet 4 subagents beat single-agent Opus 4 by 90.2% on an internal research eval; token usage explained ~80% of performance variance on BrowseComp; parallel subagents and parallel tool calls cut research time by up to 90% on complex queries. Costs: agents use ~4x chat tokens and multi-agent systems ~15x, so only high-value tasks justify it. Reliability: durable execution resuming from the failure point, retries, checkpoints, rainbow deployments, and full tracing.
papers.design_implication: Budget parallel fan-out as a token multiplier (expect 4-15x) and gate it by task value; implement durable execution with checkpoints per branch so a failed branch resumes rather than restarting the whole task; deploy new versions without disrupting in-flight DAGs.

papers.title: Prompt caching (Claude Developer Platform documentation)
papers.authors: Anthropic
papers.citation_signal: Authoritative provider documentation defining cache semantics that every fan-out must respect
papers.key_contribution: Cache writes cost 1.25x base input (5-minute TTL) or 2x (1-hour TTL); cache reads cost 0.1x (lower on some models); minimum cacheable prefix 512-4096 tokens depending on model; up to 4 explicit cache_control breakpoints; hierarchy tools -> system -> messages where a change at one level invalidates everything after it. Critically for parallelism: 'A cache entry becomes available only after the first response begins. For parallel requests that need cache hits, send the first request and wait for its response to start before sending the others.' Pre-warming via max_tokens: 0 is supported.
papers.design_implication: Fan-out scheduling must be cache-aware: issue one warm-up request (or a max_tokens: 0 prewarm) on the shared prefix, wait for first-byte, then release the burst. Keep tool definitions, system prompt and shared context byte-identical and ordered stable-first across all branches; place per-branch content after the last breakpoint.

papers.title: Rate limits (Claude Developer Platform documentation)
papers.authors: Anthropic
papers.citation_signal: Authoritative provider documentation; defines the admission-control contract clients must implement
papers.key_contribution: Limits are per model class in RPM, input tokens per minute (ITPM) and output tokens per minute (OTPM), enforced with a token bucket (continuous replenishment, so 60 RPM may be enforced as ~1 request/second and bursts fail). Exceeding returns HTTP 429 with a retry-after header; sharp usage increases hit separate acceleration limits, so traffic should ramp gradually. Cache-aware ITPM: cache_read_input_tokens do not count toward ITPM on most models (example: 2M ITPM with 80% cache hit rate yields ~10M effective input tokens/min). Response headers expose remaining requests/tokens and reset times. The Batch API has separate limits (up to 100,000 requests per batch).
papers.design_implication: Implement a client-side token bucket mirroring RPM/ITPM/OTPM per model, pre-estimating input tokens per branch and refilling from the anthropic-ratelimit-*-remaining headers; honor retry-after; ramp fan-out width up gradually; and route shared context through the cache so it does not consume ITPM.

papers.title: Batch processing (Message Batches API documentation)
papers.authors: Anthropic
papers.citation_signal: Authoritative provider documentation; defines the offline parallelism tier
papers.key_contribution: Asynchronous batches of Messages requests, each processed independently, with a 50% cost reduction and higher throughput; most batches finish in under 1 hour (results polled and retrieved when all requests end). Intended for bulk evaluations, large-scale analyses and anything that does not need immediate responses.
papers.design_implication: Give the component a 'deferred' execution tier: when the task deadline allows, route wide fan-outs (corpus-wide classification, log triage, BOM enrichment) to the Batch API at half cost instead of consuming interactive rate limits. The same DAG should be executable in interactive or batch mode by configuration.

papers.title: Function calling guide (parallel function calling)
papers.authors: OpenAI
papers.citation_signal: Authoritative provider documentation; establishes that multi-call-per-turn is the default contract across major APIs
papers.key_contribution: A single model response may contain zero, one or many function calls ('assume there are several'); parallel_tool_calls=false forces at most one. Each call carries a call_id and all outputs are returned together in one follow-up request. tool_choice supports auto, required, a forced function, allowed_tools subsets (which also preserve prompt caching) and none.
papers.design_implication: The executor must treat every model turn as a potential batch of tool calls, execute them concurrently keyed by call_id, and return all results in one turn; disable parallel calls only for tools with ordering side effects. Use allowed_tools-style restriction rather than changing the tool list to keep cache prefixes stable.

papers.title: vLLM documentation (features: continuous batching, PagedAttention, speculative decoding, prefix caching, chunked prefill)
papers.authors: vLLM project
papers.citation_signal: Documentation of the most widely deployed open-source LLM serving engine
papers.key_contribution: Lists continuous batching of incoming requests, PagedAttention KV management, speculative decoding (n-gram, suffix, EAGLE and other drafters), automatic prefix caching (enable_prefix_caching=True; reuses KV for shared prefixes across requests, speeding prefill but not decode), chunked prefill and broad quantization support. The prefix-caching page gives long-document multi-question and multi-turn chat as the target cases.
papers.design_implication: When self-hosting, enable prefix caching and speculative decoding and shape fan-out requests to share byte-identical prefixes; because prefix caching accelerates only prefill, the benefit is largest for wide fan-outs over a long shared document with short per-branch outputs, which is exactly the map phase of document map-reduce.

techniques.name: Planner-emitted DAG with dependency-aware concurrent executor (LLMCompiler / ReWOO pattern)
techniques.description: 1) A planner call receives the task prompt plus tool/sub-task schemas and emits a list of tasks, each with an id, a callable (tool or LLM sub-prompt), arguments, and references to other tasks' outputs via placeholders ($1, $2...). 2) Build a DAG from the placeholders; validate it is acyclic and that every referenced id exists. 3) A task-fetching loop maintains a ready set (all dependencies resolved); dispatch every ready task concurrently through the rate-limited executor, substitute resolved values into arguments at dispatch time. 4) As tasks complete, persist outputs (checkpoint), mark dependents ready. 5) If a task result indicates the plan is insufficient (empty result, failed validation), invoke a bounded replanner with the current partial results; otherwise, when the sink task completes, run the final synthesis call. 6) Record per-task latency to compute the critical path and the achieved speedup versus sum of task latencies.
source_titles: An LLM Compiler for Parallel Function Calling
ReWOO: Decoupling Reasoning from Observations for Efficient Augmented Language Models
Parrot: Efficient Serving of LLM-based Applications with Semantic Variable
Asynchronous LLM Function Calling
techniques.when_to_use: Any multi-step task where the steps can be enumerated before execution: multi-source lookups, multi-file code analysis, requirements-to-test traceability, enrichment of BOM lines, incident data gathering across systems.
techniques.tradeoffs: Planner adds one serial call (often the Amdahl bottleneck); plans can be wrong when tool outputs are unpredictable, requiring replanning rounds that each add latency; placeholder resolution needs strict typing to avoid injecting garbage into downstream calls. Gains documented: up to 3.7x latency and 6.7x cost versus ReAct, with equal or better accuracy.
techniques.default_parameters: Max fan-out per level: 8-16 (bounded by rate-limit bucket); max replanning rounds: 2 (LLMCompiler replans only when no candidate succeeds); per-task timeout: 2-3x the task type's observed p95; planner model: fastest model that passes a plan-validity eval (ReWOO distilled planning into a 7B model); require JSON/structured plan output and reject plans with cycles or unknown ids.

techniques.name: Skeleton-then-expand parallel generation with a suitability router (SoT-R)
techniques.description: 1) Router: classify the task prompt as 'point-independent' (lists of considerations, surveys of options, multi-aspect reviews) vs 'sequentially dependent' (derivations, code, narrative). Use a small prompt-based or fine-tuned classifier. 2) If suitable: skeleton call asks for 3-10 concise bullet headers in a fixed format. 3) Fan out one expansion call per header, all sharing the identical prefix (task + full skeleton) with the header to expand at the end, with an output length cap. 4) Concatenate in skeleton order; optionally run a cheap coherence/transition pass. 5) If unsuitable: fall back to normal sequential generation.
source_titles: Skeleton-of-Thought: Prompting LLMs for Efficient Parallel Generation
techniques.when_to_use: Long-form answers whose sections are independent: design option comparisons, risk registers, review checklists, FAQ-style documentation, multi-criteria evaluations.
techniques.tradeoffs: Up to 2.39x latency reduction (over 2x on 8 of 12 models) but reduced coherence/immersion; degrades math, coding, Fermi and writing tasks; total tokens increase (skeleton + N expansions + repeated prefix) so cost rises unless the prefix is cached. Router adds a small serial cost.
techniques.default_parameters: Skeleton length 3-10 points (paper's prompts request short point lists); per-point expansion cap ~100-200 words; temperature low for skeleton, moderate for expansions; router: prompt-based (GPT-4-class) or ~120M RoBERTa fine-tuned on annotated data; route math/coding/writing to sequential by default.

techniques.name: Adaptive sampling-and-voting ensemble (self-consistency / Agent Forest / USC) with early stopping
techniques.description: 1) Decide verifiability: exact-match (numeric, classification, code with tests) vs free-form. 2) Issue an initial batch of n0 samples concurrently at temperature > 0 (for self-hosted PagedAttention engines, request n in one call to share prompt KV). 3) Canonicalize answers with a domain-specific normalizer and tally. 4) If the leading answer has a margin >= m over the runner-up, stop; otherwise issue another batch up to n_max. 5) For free-form outputs, use Universal Self-Consistency: one aggregator call shown all candidates picks the most consistent. 6) For verifiable domains with an executable checker, scale samples further and select the first verified candidate (coverage scaling). 7) Log vote entropy as a confidence signal for downstream verification.
source_titles: Self-Consistency Improves Chain of Thought Reasoning in Language Models
More Agents Is All You Need
Universal Self-Consistency for Large Language Model Generation
Large Language Monkeys: Scaling Inference Compute with Repeated Sampling
Scaling LLM Test-Time Compute Optimally can be More Effective than Scaling Model Parameters
techniques.when_to_use: Reasoning, calculation, classification and code generation where a wrong answer is costly and tokens are cheaper than errors; also as a confidence estimator for routing to human review.
techniques.tradeoffs: Linear cost in n; gains are largest on medium-difficulty tasks and taper when the task exceeds model capacity (More Agents) or the domain is unverifiable (voting plateaus beyond several hundred samples per Large Language Monkeys). USC aggregator input grows with n x answer length. Mixed-model ensembles can lower quality (Self-MoA).
techniques.default_parameters: n0 = 5, n_max = 10 for typical tasks; 15-20 for hard tasks (13B models reached 70B-level accuracy at ~15 agents; GPT-3.5 at ~20); up to 40 in the TMLR study; early-stop margin m = 2 votes or leader >= 60% of samples; temperature 0.7 (self-consistency used sampling with temperature); USC n = 5-8; for verifiable code tasks allow 50-250 samples when a test harness exists (SWE-bench Lite coverage 15.9% -> 56% at 250). Prefer homogeneous samples from the best model (Self-MoA +6.6% over mixed MoA).

techniques.name: Branch-Solve-Merge and LLM map-reduce over documents and criteria
techniques.description: 1) Branch: either the model proposes independent sub-tasks (evaluation criteria, constraints, sections) or the system chunks a long input (fixed-token chunks with overlap, or structural chunking by section/clause/log window). 2) Map/Solve: run every branch concurrently with a shared cached prefix (global instructions + optional global summary) and a structured output schema: {extracted_evidence, rationale, answer, confidence}. 3) Reduce/Merge: if the number of branch outputs exceeds the aggregator's comfortable context, reduce hierarchically (fan-in of 5-10 per reducer) using an associative merge prompt; final reducer resolves inter-chunk conflicts by comparing calibrated confidences and cites evidence chunks. 4) Persist all map outputs so a failed reducer can rerun without re-mapping.
source_titles: Branch-Solve-Merge Improves Large Language Model Evaluation and Generation
LLM x MapReduce: Simplified Long-Sequence Processing using Large Language Models
MapReduce: Simplified Data Processing on Large Clusters
Building effective agents
techniques.when_to_use: Multi-criteria evaluation (LLM-as-judge), multi-constraint generation, and any input larger than a comfortable context: standards documents, requirement sets, long test logs, incident timelines, large codebases.
techniques.tradeoffs: Loses cross-chunk dependencies (mitigate with overlap, a global summary pass, or a structured info protocol) and can surface conflicting answers (mitigate with confidence calibration in the reducer). BSM improved human-LLM agreement up to 26% and cut position/length bias up to 50%; LLM x MapReduce outperformed long-context models but adds a reduce stage of serial latency.
techniques.default_parameters: Chunk size: largest that leaves headroom for instructions and output (commonly 4k-16k tokens) with 10-15% overlap for prose, zero overlap for structurally delimited data; fan-in per reducer 5-10; map temperature 0; require confidence on a fixed scale (e.g., 1-5) and evidence quotes; number of branches for BSM-style evaluation typically 3-6 criteria proposed by the model.

techniques.name: Layered proposer-aggregator ensemble (Mixture-of-Agents / Archon-searched topology)
techniques.description: 1) Layer 1: k proposer calls run concurrently on the task. 2) Layer l>1: each proposer receives the task plus all layer l-1 outputs and produces an improved response (concurrent within the layer). 3) Final aggregator receives the last layer's outputs with an instruction to critically synthesize, correct errors, and not merely average. 4) Optionally replace heterogeneous proposers with k samples of the single best model (Self-MoA). 5) Treat {layers, k, proposer set, aggregator, optional verifier/ranker} as a searchable configuration and tune it offline on a domain eval set under a token budget.
source_titles: Mixture-of-Agents Enhances Large Language Model Capabilities
Rethinking Mixture-of-Agents: Is Mixing Different Large Language Models Beneficial?
Archon: An Architecture Search Framework for Inference-Time Techniques
Improving Factuality and Reasoning in Language Models through Multiagent Debate
techniques.when_to_use: High-value, latency-tolerant generation where quality matters more than cost: design review summaries, root-cause analyses, specification drafting, safety-critical recommendations.
techniques.tradeoffs: MoA reached 65.1% AlpacaEval 2.0 vs 57.5% GPT-4o but layers are sequential (high TTFT) and cost scales as layers x k; mixing weaker models can reduce quality (Self-MoA beats MoA by 6.6%). Archon shows searched topologies beat frontier single models by 15.1% on average but search needs an eval set.
techniques.default_parameters: Start with MoA-Lite: 2 layers, 3-6 proposers, strongest model as aggregator; full MoA used 3 layers x 6 proposers; Self-MoA default: k=6 samples of the best model at temperature ~0.7; aggregator temperature 0; enable heterogeneous proposers only when each proposer's standalone eval score is within a few points of the best.

techniques.name: Resilient rate-limited async executor: token bucket, full-jitter backoff, retry budget, circuit breaker, bulkheads, deadlines
techniques.description: 1) Admission: a client-side token bucket per (provider, model) tracking RPM, input-tokens/min and output-tokens/min; estimate input tokens per request before dispatch, acquire capacity or wait; refresh capacity from provider rate-limit response headers. 2) Concurrency: a bulkhead (semaphore) per model and per tool so one slow dependency cannot exhaust the pool. 3) Retry: on 429/529/5xx/timeouts, sleep = max(retry_after, random(0, min(cap, base * 2^attempt))); at most 3 attempts per request; a global retry budget rejecting retries once retries exceed 10% of recent requests; never retry 4xx validation errors. 4) Circuit breaker per endpoint: open after a failure-rate threshold in a sliding window, fail fast while open, half-open probe after a cooldown. 5) Deadlines: every DAG run has a deadline propagated to each branch minus a margin; branches past their deadline are cancelled along with hedged duplicates. 6) Criticality tags: shed speculative/hedged/extra-ensemble work before primary branches under pressure. 7) Idempotency keys on side-effecting tool calls so re-execution after failure is safe.
source_titles: Exponential Backoff And Jitter
Site Reliability Engineering: Handling Overload; Addressing Cascading Failures
Release It! Second Edition: Design and Deploy Production-Ready Software
Rate limits (Claude Developer Platform documentation)
MapReduce: Simplified Data Processing on Large Clusters
techniques.when_to_use: Always; this is the substrate every other technique runs on.
techniques.tradeoffs: Adds client complexity and some latency for admission; too-aggressive breakers cause unnecessary fail-fast; retry budgets trade a few failed requests for protection against retry storms (worst-case amplification ~1.1x instead of 3x). Without jitter, N branches that fail together retry together and re-collide.
techniques.default_parameters: Attempts per request: 3 (SRE); retry budget: 10% of requests (SRE); client adaptive throttling K=2 (SRE); backoff base 0.5-1s, cap 20-60s with full jitter (Brooker); honor retry-after as a floor; circuit breaker: open at >=50% failures over a 20-request window or 5 consecutive failures, half-open after 30s (Nygard gives the pattern; thresholds are common practice); queue depth <= 50% of worker pool for steady traffic (SRE); ramp fan-out gradually to avoid provider acceleration limits; deadline margin a few hundred ms per hop (SRE).

techniques.name: Prompt-cache-aware fan-out (warm-then-burst) with stable shared prefix
techniques.description: 1) Structure every branch's request as [tools][system][shared context]...[branch-specific suffix], with cache_control on the last shared block; keep tools/system/context byte-identical across branches and do not vary tool_choice, thinking or effort settings. 2) Before releasing the fan-out, send one warm-up request on the shared prefix (either the first real branch, or a max_tokens: 0 prewarm) and wait until its response begins. 3) Release the remaining branches concurrently; verify cache_read_input_tokens > 0 in responses and alert on misses. 4) Schedule follow-up phases (e.g., reduce after map) within the TTL or use the 1-hour TTL when phases are more than 5 minutes apart. 5) On self-hosted vLLM/SGLang, enable prefix caching so RadixAttention/APC reuses the shared KV.
source_titles: Prompt caching (Claude Developer Platform documentation)
Rate limits (Claude Developer Platform documentation)
SGLang: Efficient Execution of Structured Language Model Programs
vLLM documentation (features: continuous batching, PagedAttention, speculative decoding, prefix caching, chunked prefill)
techniques.when_to_use: Every fan-out whose branches share more than the minimum cacheable prefix (long system prompt, tool schemas, a shared document, a skeleton or plan).
techniques.tradeoffs: The warm-up adds one time-to-first-byte of latency before the burst; cache writes cost 1.25x (or 2x for 1h TTL) so single-use prefixes should not be cached; misordered content or a changed tool definition invalidates everything after it. Benefit: reads cost ~0.1x and do not count toward ITPM on most models, which can multiply effective throughput (2M ITPM at 80% hit rate -> ~10M effective).
techniques.default_parameters: Shared prefix >= 1024 tokens (512 on the newest models) to be cacheable; up to 4 breakpoints; 5-minute TTL by default, 1-hour for phase gaps > 5 min; warm-up wait = first streamed token of the warm-up request; target cache hit rate for fan-outs > 80%.

techniques.name: Hedged requests and straggler mitigation for fan-out tail latency
techniques.description: 1) Track per-(model, request-class) latency distributions online. 2) For each idempotent branch, if no response has begun by the class's p95, issue a duplicate (optionally to a different region/provider or a faster model with equivalent output contract) and take the first completion; cancel the loser. 3) Cap hedges to a small fraction of requests and count them as SHEDDABLE under rate-limit pressure. 4) For the DAG as a whole, mark straggler branches past the deadline and let the aggregator proceed with partial results plus an explicit 'missing branch' notice, when the task's quality contract allows. 5) Never hedge non-idempotent tool calls; use idempotency keys if duplication is possible.
source_titles: The Tail at Scale
Site Reliability Engineering: Handling Overload; Addressing Cascading Failures
MapReduce: Simplified Data Processing on Large Clusters
techniques.when_to_use: Wide fan-outs (>= 5 branches) with user-facing latency targets; the completion time of a fan-out is the max over branches, so per-branch tail dominates.
techniques.tradeoffs: Extra load (bounded by the hedge fraction) and wasted tokens for cancelled duplicates (streaming lets you cancel early); hedging on providers without cancellation still bills the loser; proceeding with partial results trades completeness for latency.
techniques.default_parameters: Hedge trigger at the observed p95 latency for that request class (Dean & Barroso); hedge fraction cap ~5% of requests; deadline per branch = 2-3x median; partial-result threshold: aggregator proceeds when >= 80% of branches complete and the deadline is reached, else fails the task.

techniques.name: Amdahl-driven critical-path budgeting and parallel-mode selection
techniques.description: 1) Instrument every run: record per-node latency and dependencies; compute critical path length C and total work W. 2) Estimate the serial fraction (1-p) = latency of planner + aggregator + any serial chain, over total sequential latency. 3) Predicted speedup bound = 1/(1-p); if measured speedup is near the bound, further fan-out is pointless and effort should go to shortening planner/aggregator (smaller model, streaming, cached prefix, deterministic code merge). 4) Use the routing table: (a) independent enumerable subtasks -> DAG executor; (b) point-independent long-form -> skeleton-expand; (c) single answer with verifier or exact match -> sampling-and-voting; (d) long input -> map-reduce; (e) high-value free-form -> layered ensemble; (f) sequentially dependent reasoning -> no parallelism. 5) Combine with the deferred tier: when the deadline permits, send the fan-out to the Batch API at 50% cost instead of consuming interactive capacity.
